questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Applying for a post and the phrase that asks for it
questions.learningObjective: identify the verb and its object in a request for employment
questions.stem: A letter asking for a place in a company opens 'Me dirijo a usted para solicitar...'. Which completion states the act the letter is actually making?

options.text: The post itself, because solicitar is transitive and takes the thing applied for as its object
The hours worked in that job, because solicitar always names a schedule rather than a place
options.misconception: believes solicitar is followed by the working hours instead of the post being applied for

options.text: A meeting with the manager, because a written request of this kind replaces the interview
options.misconception: treats the written application as a substitute for the interview rather than a step before it

options.text: The company's own accounts, since every applicant must declare a firm's finances
options.misconception: confuses a job application with a declaration about the employer's business

questions.explanation: The rule here is the direct object. Solicitar, like pedir and exigir, is transitive: it is followed immediately by the noun naming what is requested, with no preposition, so solicitar el puesto is grammatical and solicitar del puesto is not. That is why the sentence can name the job and nothing else, and why the four word slots available after the preposition of the offer all have to be the noun the writer actually wants. The trap option assumes a second noun in the phrase, which is what happens with a different verb: a native reader is as comfortable with me dirijo a usted para solicitar una cita as with the post, because the object is whatever the request is about. The letter therefore states one concrete act, and the wording is chosen so that no reader can take it for a request about pay, hours or a meeting, because a preposition or a wrong noun would have spoiled the claim.
questions.hint: Ask what noun sits straight after solicitar, and whether a preposition separates them.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A CV and the block it leads with
questions.learningObjective: read what a CV foregrounds by the order of its blocks
questions.stem: A CV puts a short block of 'aptitudes' first: gestión de equipo, atención al cliente, resolución de problemas. What has that writer put at the top?

options.text: A claim about what they can already do, placed ahead of the record that supports it
The years of study, because a reader checks qualifications before anything else
options.misconception: assumes a reader opens a CV with the date of the degree rather than the claim

options.text: A list of former employers, so the whole career can be dated from the first line
options.misconception: believes the first block of a CV exists to name employers rather than to claim ability

options.text: A figure for the salary expected, since that is the one number a reader looks for
options.misconception: supposes a salary figure belongs in a CV rather than in a later conversation

questions.explanation: Order in a CV is argument, not decoration. Whatever block comes first is the claim the rest of the document is offered to support, and a list of aptitudes is a claim about present ability, so placing it above the dates asks the reader to read the record as evidence rather than as the news. Aptitudes is itself the vocabulary of the office: it names capacities that an employer can compare against a job description, which is why the heading is used rather than the heading of hobbies. The other blocks have their own place, since qualifications and previous employers are what the aptitudes rest on, and moving them to the front would turn the document into a chronology. A salary figure does not belong in the CV at all in the Spanish market, since the figure is normally discussed at a later stage, and a reader who expects to find it there has imported an expectation from a different kind of document.
questions.hint: Ask which block the rest of the document is there to support.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: You and usted in an interview room
questions.learningObjective: tell the polite forms of address from the familiar ones
questions.stem: In an interview the chair of the panel says 'Dígame usted cómo fue su primer día en el puesto'. Which pronoun does that polite command actually use?

options.text: Usted, because the polite imperative is built on the third person pronoun of courtesy
Tú, because every command in Spanish is built on the second person pronoun
options.misconception: assumes the imperative is always formed on tú and never on a courtesy pronoun

options.text: Vosotros, because a panel that asks one question speaks for a group
options.misconception: reads a plural group meaning into a form addressed to one person

options.text: Vos, because the interviewer has met the candidate before today
options.misconception: takes a prior meeting to change the pronoun of address to the voseo form

questions.explanation: The rule is that the Spanish imperative has two sources. A verb in the second person singular gives the familiar form, di game becomes dime, and a verb in the third person gives the polite form, diga becomes dígame. What decides between them is the pronoun of address, so the choice of usted in the second half of the sentence fixes the first half of it. Vos is a separate system found in parts of Latin America, where it replaces the second person pronoun in the address itself, and vosotros is the second person plural used in Spain, so neither is what a chair of a panel uses with one candidate. The two pronouns in this sentence are usted twice, which is what a careful speaker keeps, and the register is set by that repetition rather than by the greeting at the door.
questions.hint: Look at the pronoun after the verb, then check which person the command is built on.

questions.topic: A cover letter and the relationship its closing claims
questions.learningObjective: read the relationship a closing formula assumes between writer and reader
questions.stem: A cover letter ends 'Quedo a la espera de su respuesta y le agradezco su atención'. What relationship between the two sides is that closing claiming?

options.text: A continuing one, since it treats the reader as a person who is going to answer
A finished one, because gratitude is the standard way of closing any letter at all
options.misconception: reads a formula of politeness as a statement that the matter is already closed

options.text: A contractual one, because a promise of an answer has the force of a signed agreement
options.misconception: believes a set politeness formula can bind the reader to a reply

options.text: An equal one, because the writer uses the form that a friend would use in a message
options.misconception: confuses the register of a formal letter with the register of a message to a peer

questions.explanation: The rule to read here is the tense and the person of the closing formula. Quedo a la espera is present tense, and the speaker puts their own waiting in the same time as the answer that has not yet come, so the letter treats the exchange as unfinished. The agreement of le, in singular, is the form used with usted, which is the polite second person and signals distance rather than equality. The gratitude then names the reader's time as the gift, and a formula of that kind appears in a business letter precisely because the writer cannot yet assume a reply. The trap reading takes the set phrase as automatic and empty, when in fact the same words would sound wrong in a message to a friend, which is the test that shows the register is doing work here.
questions.hint: Ask what tense the waiting is in, and which person the agreement is with.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A clause of a job contract
questions.learningObjective: read a clause of a contract and say what period it names
questions.stem: A contract begins 'Durante un período de prueba de tres meses, el trabajo se considerará en período de adaptación'. Which clause is the phrase naming?

options.text: A trial stretch with a stated end, before the arrangement is treated as settled
The warning each side must give, counted backwards from the end of the contract
options.misconception: confuses the trial period with the notice period and puts the two in one clause

options.text: A term in which the employee must train for a qualification the work requires
options.misconception: reads a period of settling into the job as a period of formal study

options.text: Leave without pay, which the employer grants in place of a salary for a time
options.misconception: supposes unpaid leave and a trial period are two names for one thing

questions.explanation: The rule is the two uses of de in un período de prueba de tres meses. The first de links a general noun to the type it belongs to, as in una sala de reuniones, and the second links the same noun to the measure of it, as in una reunión de dos horas. Período de prueba is therefore the trial period by definition, and the three months are how long it lasts, which is why the phrase sets an end and not a condition. The accent is part of the same care: período carries a written accent because the stress falls on the antepenult syllable, pe-rio-do, and without it the word would be read as a llana with the stress on the last syllable, which is a different word. A clause about notice belongs at the end of a contract and counts differently, and a clause about unpaid leave carries a different consequence altogether, so neither can be what this opening sentence names.
questions.hint: Ask whether each de links a type or a measure, and whether the clause sets an end.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: The word for a monthly pay slip
questions.learningObjective: read the definite article as marking a single monthly payment
questions.stem: An employee says 'Este mes me pagan la nómina más baja del año'. Which reading does that sentence actually give?

options.text: One month's pay, named by the document that records it and compared with the other months
A cut agreed for the whole year, since the definite article marks the entire period
options.misconception: takes the definite article as marking a year-wide reduction rather than one month

options.text: A bonus added at the year end in return for results reached in December
options.misconception: reads a regular monthly payment as an end-of-year reward

options.text: An advance from the firm, repaid by instalments out of each month's pay
options.misconception: confuses the pay slip with a loan that the employee repays monthly

questions.explanation: La nómina is the document on which an employer records what is paid, and metían la nómina is the ordinary phrase for being paid, so the word has come to stand for the payment itself. The definite article does the work that la often does elsewhere: it is not marking something known only to the two speakers but the single instance under discussion, and the comparison superlative más baja then shows that this instance is being ranked against the other months. Este mes at the front fixes the comparison, so the sentence is about a slice of the year and not about the year. A reduction agreed for the whole period would be expressed as a noun of its own with a different verb, and an advance would be named as one, which is why neither of those readings survives the wording.
questions.hint: Ask which single thing the article is picking out, and what este mes is comparing it with.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Names of shifts in a duty rota
questions.learningObjective: read a shift label and say what period it covers
questions.stem: A hospital rota lists 'Turno de noche: 22.00 a 6.00' and 'Turno de mañana: 8.00 a 15.00'. What do these two labels name?

options.text: The stretch of hours a person is on duty, which the two clock times delimit
The weekday on which the shift falls in a given week of the rota
options.misconception: reads a block of hours as a day of the week

options.text: The group a worker belongs to for a whole month in that department
options.misconception: treats a label that pairs hours with a time of day as a team name

options.text: The number of people needed to cover the same hours on that night
options.misconception: believes the label counts staff rather than marking the period itself

questions.explanation: The grammar that fixes the reading is the de before the noun of time, and a Spanish time noun normally follows de: turno de noche, turno de tarde, turno de mañana. That de is the same linking particle seen in a sala de reuniones, and it marks the kind of the block, not the day. The two clock times then do the measuring, since twenty-two to six is a block that crosses midnight and eight to fifteen is one that does not, so the pair is enough to fix the length without a word of headcount. The vocabulary of the office distinguishes three such labels and expects everyone on the ward to know them, which is why a rota can be printed with no legend at all. A day of the week is named with a day noun, a team is named with a noun of people, and a staffing figure is a number, so none of those could occupy the slot this phrase fills.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two clock times are measuring something, and what the de links.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Saying that someone is off work sick
questions.learningObjective: choose between ser and estar for a temporary state
questions.stem: A colleague has been off sick for a month. Which sentence reports that in the standard way?

options.text: Está de baja, because a temporary state in someone's working life takes estar
Es de baja, because anything said about the state of a person takes ser
options.misconception: believes ser covers the whole field of personal circumstances

options.text: Está de bajas, because the phrase takes a plural noun after the preposition de
options.misconception: makes the phrase plural on the grounds that a month is a long stretch

options.text: Es baja, because baja functions as an adjective and not as a noun in this phrase
options.misconception: reads the word as an adjective and drops the preposition the phrase needs

questions.explanation: The rule is the division of labour between the two copulas. Ser names what something is and is used for a category, an origin, a profession or a material, whereas estar names a state that a thing or a person is in at a moment, and being off work is exactly such a state because it is expected to end. De baja is a noun, so the phrase is de baja and not a bare baja, and a single state is singular even when it has lasted a month, since the length of a state does not make its number change. The copula swap in the first distractor is the mistake that a learner makes most often with this family of phrases, and it matters because es de baja would describe what somebody permanently is, which is not what the sentence reports at all.
questions.hint: Ask whether the situation is expected to end, and whether the phrase needs de.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A CV line about how long a skill has been used
questions.learningObjective: read the present of llevar with a gerund as duration still running
questions.stem: A CV line says 'Llevo seis años trabajando en atención al cliente'. What does the present of the verb add to that statement?

options.text: A stretch of time that began in the past and is still going at the moment of speaking
A habit that stopped at some point last year, since the present marks a finished period
options.misconception: reads the present of llevar as marking a stretch that has already closed

options.text: An intention not yet begun, since the gerund places the action after the reading of the line
options.misconception: treats the gerund after llevar as marking an action that has not started

options.text: A length of time that counts from the start of the year and stops at its end
options.misconception: supposes the time expression in the sentence fixes a calendar period rather than a duration

questions.explanation: The rule is the pairing of the present of llevar with a gerund, which is one of the two ways Spanish counts duration. Llevar in the present, followed by a gerund and a time expression, says that the action started at a point in the past and has not stopped: llevo seis años trabajando means six years and counting, not six years. A gerund in Spanish is not an English one, since it does not say that the action happens at the moment of speaking, and the action is in progress in exactly the same way whether the verb before it is llevar or estar. That is the trap the fourth option takes, importing a reading of the gerund that the Spanish form does not have. The alternative form of counting, hacer plus a time phrase, would start a different sentence, and mixing the two constructions inside one line is what makes the sentence hard to read.
questions.hint: Ask whether the action has stopped, and what the present tense of the verb does with it.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Reporting a fault without naming anyone at fault
questions.learningObjective: recognise the construction that makes the affected person the grammatical subject
questions.stem: A worker says 'Se me ha roto la máquina de la oficina'. Who does that sentence hold responsible for the breakage?

options.text: Nobody in particular, since the construction puts the sufferer in front and leaves the cause out
Whoever used it last, because a passive pointing at a thing names the person who operated it
options.misconception: supposes a passive with a machine as its subject must identify the last operator

options.text: The office itself, since a machine stands for the building where it stands
options.misconception: reads a metonym for a place as a claim about who is at fault

options.text: The maintenance firm, because every fault ends in a repair invoice and so a culprit
options.misconception: infers the guilty party from a commercial consequence rather than from the sentence

questions.explanation: The rule is the se construction with a dative of the person affected, and the diagnostic is the order of the two pronouns. When the pronoun that refers to a person comes first, me precedes lo, and the phrase carries the sufferer: se me ha roto, se nos ha caído, se les ha estropeado. The verb is the same verb in all of them, the subject slot is taken by se, and the real subject of the event, whatever broke, is left unsaid. That is the point of the construction, since it reports a bad luck that happened to the speaker without accusing anybody, which is why it is the polite way to mention a fault in a workplace. Nothing in the sentence supports a name, and inferring one from who eventually fixes the machine is reading a whole story into a single clause.
questions.hint: Look at the order of the two pronouns in the sentence, and ask who is being spared.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A union and what it negotiates
questions.learningObjective: say what a union's central activity is and with whom
questions.stem: A workers' organisation describes itself as 'el sindicato que negocia el convenio con la empresa'. Which activity does that phrase name?

options.text: Bargaining with the employer over the collective agreement, on behalf of members
Supervising staff on the employer's behalf to make sure output is met
options.misconception: reads a bargaining body as an agent of management

options.text: Granting qualifications recognised by the state after an apprenticeship
options.misconception: confuses negotiation over pay and conditions with the award of credentials

options.text: Issuuing the published rules that individual contracts must follow
options.misconception: treats a union's agreement as if it were a set of general regulations

questions.explanation: Negociar takes a preposition naming who is negotiated with, and convenio names the collective agreement that in Spain is drawn up between the representatives of the workers and those of the company, often with the law's requirements in view. The verb is the whole of the claim: to bargain, not to administer, certify or publish. A union's function in a workplace is representative, so what it produces binds the members as well as the employer, which is why the agreement is called a collective one and not a private contract between one firm and one worker. A body that supervised output for the employer would be management by another name, and qualification-awarding belongs to a training body, while a set of published rules comes from whoever has the power to make them, which is why the phrase is read from the inside rather than the outside.
questions.hint: Ask which preposition the verb takes, and who both sides of the agreement are.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: The steps a labour dispute passes through
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of a collective dispute
questions.stem: Five stages of a collective labour dispute have been listed out of order. Which sequence is the order the process actually passes through?

options.text: A demand formulated by the workers' representatives
A failed attempt to settle the matter inside the workplace
A conciliation step before a conciliation body outside the firm
A call for a stoppage in the work, taken by vote
An agreement, or a ruling if the parties never agree on one

questions.explanation: The order follows the escalation of the body that hears the case. A demand comes first, because there is nothing to answer until the workers' side has said what it wants, and it is put to the employer inside the firm, where the matter should be settled if it is going to be settled informally. If the firm does not answer or refuses, the case leaves the workplace, and a conciliation step before a body outside it is the next stage, since a neutral meeting is cheaper for everyone than a stoppage. Only when that fails does a stoppage get called, and that is a vote because it costs every member pay. The last stage is either a settlement or a ruling, and the sequence matters because each step assumes the previous one has run its course, so a process that began with the stoppage would skip the two stages built to avoid it.
questions.hint: Ask what has to fail before the next step becomes possible.

questions.learningObjective: choose the polite and possessive forms when asking for information
questions.stem: An employee asks the manager '¿Me podría decir cuál es su salario base?'. What do the forms of the two pronouns do here?

questions.topic: A safety rule and the reason printed next to it
questions.learningObjective: read a prohibition and its justification as two parts of one rule

questions.topic: Saying when a shift will start
questions.learningObjective: read a time conjunction that takes the subjunctive
questions.stem: A note on a rota reads 'En cuanto llegue el nuevo técnico, empezaré el turno de mañana'. What is the speaker committing to?

questions.topic: Proposing a change in working arrangements
questions.learningObjective: read a conditional of gustar as a polite proposal
questions.stem: An employee writes 'Me gustaría trabajar dos días a la semana desde casa'. What is the sentence doing?

questions.topic: Why a public holiday carries two origins at once

questions.stem: Explain why a public holiday in Spain can be at once a religious feast and a civic commemoration, and say what each of the two parts is doing in the calendar.

answer.exemplar: The two parts come from two different authorities writing on the same calendar. The religious part arrives from the Church, which fixes the date of a feast in the liturgical year, and a Catholic country inherited that rhythm early, so a saint's day was a day of rest before it was a day of any state. The civic part is a later addition: when a state wanted a moment of its own, it could not move a feast that half the country already kept, so it put its commemoration on the day that was there. That is why a holiday can carry both meanings and why a person who is not religious still observes it. Each part does something different in the calendar. The feast supplies the date and the habit, and it tells the country where in the year it stands, while the commemoration supplies the content, and it is the moment at which a state says what it wants to be remembered for. The two also fail separately, which is worth noticing: a state that loses interest in its commemoration leaves the day as a day off, and a country whose Church calendar thins out finds itself celebrating a civic event on a date that no longer means anything to anybody.

options.misconception: assumes every notice period is measured in days worked

options.text: A length that either side may shorten by agreement whenever it likes
options.misconception: turns a stated period into something left to the parties' convenience

options.text: A period of about a month, rounded down to a fortnight of working time
options.misconception: recalculates a stated figure in units the clause does not use

questions.explanation: The last word of the phrase does the work, and that is why it is there. Días naturales is the ordinary way of counting days in a calendar, so the fifteen runs through the Saturdays and Sundays, while días hábiles would have excluded them and a clause that says quince días naturales has deliberately chosen the longer measure. The preposition de marks the quantity in the ordinary way, de quince días, and the word preaviso names the notice itself rather than the period the employee works. A reader checking a last date therefore counts fifteen days on a calendar and not ten working ones, and getting this wrong by four days is the kind of error that decides whether an employee has served the notice. The fourth trap is the one a person in a hurry actually makes, and the third is a claim about flexibility that the clause nowhere makes.
questions.hint: Ask whether the last word contrasts with the alternative of working days only.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Two tenses in a worker's account of starting a job
questions.learningObjective: read the preterite against the imperfect in an account of a past period
questions.stem: A worker says 'Cuando llegué a la empresa, esperaba otra cosa y nadie me explicó nada'. What is the second verb doing?

options.text: Describing a state that held over a stretch of time before it changed
Saying the expectation existed and was then taken away
options.misconception: reads a state that held as though something had removed it

options.text: Saying the expectation lasted a number of minutes
options.misconception: treats the tense as though it fixed the length of the period

options.text: Reporting what the worker later discovered to be the case
options.misconception: moves an expectation into a later finding about the truth

questions.explanation: The two tenses mark two different kinds of past. Llegué is the preterite of a single completed event with a date attached, and esperaba is the imperfect of a situation that held while the worker was there, with no start and no end marked at all. Together they are the ordinary pairing for an account of a first period at work: one moment, then the state that moment put the person in. The imperfect is the tense of background, of habit and of what was true in general, which is why it is also the tense used for things that were repeated or that lasted without anybody noting the day they began. The traps all try to give the tense a job it does not do: to report a loss, to count a duration, or to reveal a truth discovered later. A learner who uses only the preterite here produces a list of events where the sentence is really about a state.
questions.hint: Ask whether the second clause gives an event with a date or a situation that lasted.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Two ways of naming the same condition in a notice
questions.learningObjective: tell a general relative from one that points at a known person
questions.stem: Two notices read 'Quien llegue después de las nueve no podrá entrar' and 'El que llegue después de las nueve no podrá entrar'. What changes between them?

options.text: Quien is general and impersonal, while el que points at somebody already identified
The two sentences say the same thing, and the difference is only one of spelling
options.misconception: supposes two different reference patterns are a typographical matter

options.text: Quien is used where the reader is unknown and el que where the reader is known
options.misconception: confuses the identity of the reader with the identity of the person referred to

options.text: El que is compulsory after a preposition and quien is never allowed there
options.misconception: reverses the rule about the relative pronoun after a preposition

questions.explanation: The rule is whether the relative word has an antecedent. Quien with no antecedent at all is a generic relative and takes the verb in the third person singular, as in quien llega tarde no entra, so it is a rule about anybody. El que keeps the article and refers back to a person already mentioned, as in el que llegue tarde, where the reader knows which person is meant. A useful extension is the rule after a preposition: a relative pronoun there is always el que and never quien, so el sitio en el que trabaja and la razón por la que no vino are both correct, and quien is not an option in either. The second trap is the one a learner is most tempted by, since the two notices are interchangeable in a corridor, and the fourth reverses a rule that is easy to remember once stated. What differs is the reference, not the sense of the condition.
questions.hint: Ask whether either relative word has a word in front of it that it points back to.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: An equality plan and what it commits a company to
questions.learningObjective: read a dated commitment as a process rather than as a result
questions.stem: A document states that a company has a plan with measures on equal pay, on promotion and on harassment, and that the plan is reviewed each year. What has the document committed the company to?

options.text: A process of measuring and revising, with dates attached to the measures
A result, since the document reports that equality has been reached
options.misconception: reads a plan as though it were a finding about the outcome

options.text: A set of posts reserved in advance for each group of employees
options.misconception: turns a commitment to measure into a fixed allocation of posts

options.text: A complaints procedure for staff to use against one another
options.misconception: reduces a whole plan to the one part about how a dispute is heard

questions.explanation: The document is a plan and a plan is a set of things to be done, so the useful reading is the one about process. The three measures name the fields in which the company has agreed to look, and the yearly review is the part that makes the document mean anything, since a set of measures examined once and then forgotten is a statement of intention. A reader who wants to know whether the company has succeeded has to wait for a later version of the document, which is the whole design of this kind of text. The second trap takes the existence of a plan to be a report of a result, and the third supplies an instrument, reserved posts, that a plan of this kind does not use. The fourth reduces three fields to one procedure, and a company can have a thorough process for handling a complaint while knowing nothing at all about what the figures show.
questions.hint: Ask what the yearly review is for, and whether the document reports a finding or a set of tasks.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A closed question on an application form
questions.learningObjective: read a form that asks a closed question before asking for detail
questions.stem: An online application offers two boxes under '¿Ha trabajado antes en este sector?' and then a box marked 'Explique su respuesta'. What is the form doing?

options.text: Asking a closed question first, and asking for detail only where it changes the answer
Asking the same thing twice, once in a short form and once at length
options.misconception: treats a request for explanation as a second question of the same kind

options.text: Making the explanation optional for every applicant alike
options.misconception: misses that the follow-up is conditional on the first answer

options.text: Ruling out in advance anyone who answers the first question in the negative
options.misconception: turns a routing question into an automatic disqualification

questions.explanation: A form is designed to make somebody answer the easy question first, and the design shows in the order. The closed question has two boxes and can be answered in a second, and the explanation box is there for the applicant whose answer makes a difference, so the form is asking for information in the order a reader can supply it. The interrogative carries the first question and the verb in the perfect tense carries the whole of its content: whether the person has already worked in that sector, and not whether the job was done well, since that is what the explanation is for. The fourth reading is a real concern in recruitment and the form does nothing to answer it, because a question with two boxes is a way of gathering information and not a test. A reader who assumes the design implies a rule will apply the rule to a form that never states one.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two boxes changes what the applicant has to write next.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Two lives of the verb poder in a workplace
questions.learningObjective: explain the two uses of poder and what the polite one promises
questions.stem: Explain why the verb poder is so widely used in a Spanish workplace, and say what its polite use does and does not promise.

answer.exemplar: Two different sentences are hiding inside the same verb, and a learner who finds only the first will overstate what Spanish promises. The first is a modal of ability: puede means the person is capable of the action, and it says nothing at all about whether they will do it. The second is a courtesy form, and it is the one to look at. Aquí puede es fórmula, means here you have, and the modal has stopped describing an ability altogether and has become a way of giving the other person the floor. The same happens in a question: ¿Puede decirme la hora is not a question about whether the addressee is able to tell the time, it is a question about whether the addressee will do it, and the person who asks knows perfectly well that the time can be told. That is the whole of the politeness, and it is worth naming for what it is, because the promise is thin. The modal gives no undertaking about what will happen next; it makes the request easy to put and easy to decline, and that difference is the difference between a request and a claim. A good answer will add that this courtesy form is one of several ways of softening an imperative in Spanish, and that a request which could be made bluntly is nearly always made in one of these ways instead, which is what makes the form feel obligatory rather than optional.

questions.hint: Ask whether the modal is reporting an ability or giving the other person a turn to speak.

questions.explanation: A good answer needs both senses of the verb separated, because that is the whole difficulty, and the second sense is the one a learner will not expect. Puede as a modal of ability reports a capacity and says nothing about action, and the courtesy form is a use where the modal has stopped describing anybody's capacity at all and has become a way of opening a turn: ¿Puede decirme la hora is a question about whether somebody will do something the asker knows can be done. The rest of the answer should name what the courtesy form actually promises, which is very little, since it makes the request easy to put and easy to refuse and it undertakes nothing about what follows. Adding that this is one of several softening devices in Spanish, and that a request which could be made bluntly is nearly always softened, completes the picture and explains why the form feels compulsory rather than optional.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Two prepositions that distinguish the place from the employer
questions.learningObjective: tell a preposition of place from a preposition of benefit
questions.stem: Explain why 'trabaja en una empresa' and 'trabaja para una empresa' say different things about the employer's business, and say which preposition names the place and which names the beneficiary.

answer.exemplar: The two prepositions select the two things a sentence about work has to name, and both of them are true at once in most jobs, which is exactly what makes the difference hard to see. En names the place, the establishment, the building or the organisation, so trabaja en una empresa tells the reader where the work is done and implies little about who profits from it; the preposition is the one of location, and it would be equally natural with a room, a city or a street. Para names the person for whom the work is done, so trabaja para una empresa is a claim about an employer, and it can be said of somebody working from home for a firm whose offices are in another country. The two can be joined in one sentence without any awkwardness, and a good answer will point out that this is the normal case, because a person normally works in a place and for a payer's account at the same time. Where the contrast becomes sharp is a job with a remote employer, and there the sentence in is simply not available, which is a neat way of showing that the prepositions are doing different work. A related pair worth naming in passing is en and para before a verb of movement, where en gives the destination inside a place and para gives the destination as a point of arrival.

questions.hint: Ask whether the preposition answers where or on whose account.

questions.explanation: The answer should assign each preposition a job and then use the normal case of the two being true at once to show the assignment is right. En names the place and is the same preposition that would go with a room, a city or a street, so trabaja en una empresa tells a reader where the work is done. Para names the person for whom the work is done, so trabaja para una empresa is a claim about an employer and can be said of somebody working from home. A good answer will point out that the contrast becomes visible precisely in the remote case, where en is simply unavailable, and may add the related contrast before a verb of movement, where en gives a destination inside a place and para gives a point of arrival. questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Dividing three costs with a flatmate
questions.learningObjective: write a proposal inside a word limit and name what it leaves unresolved
questions.stem: Stage one: write in Spanish, in no more than thirty words, a message to the person you share a flat with, proposing how three monthly costs are to be divided. Stage two: say what your message leaves open and who has to settle it.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: Propongo que dividamos el alquiler, la luz y el agua a partes iguales, y que el recibo de la luz me lo pases antes del día cinco. Stage two: the message leaves open what happens when one of you is away for a month, whether the water is metred or divided by head, and what happens to the arrangement if a bill comes out higher than usual, so three things go to a conversation. The proposal is the easy half and the second stage is where the item lives, because a division agreed in principle still has to be applied to a real bill. The grammar is doing quiet work. Propongo que dividamos is a proposal clause, and its verb is the subjunctive, which is not optional: the thing being proposed is not a fact yet, and the subjunctive is the Spanish way of saying so. A better message would add one sentence about a month when somebody travels, and a worse one would explain why the split should be equal rather than by size, which is the one question a message of this length always provokes.

questions.hint: Ask what happens to the split in a month when one of you is not there.

questions.explanation: The two stages are arranged so that the first cannot be completed well without noticing the second, and a learner asked only for the first will write a friendly message and stop at the arithmetic. The real difficulty of a shared budget is the case that the split does not cover, which is a month when one of them is away or when a bill comes out higher than usual, and a good answer names that case as the thing the message has left to a conversation. The grammar is worth drawing out, because the proposal clause and its subjunctive are what make the sentence a proposal rather than a statement, and a message that used the indicative would be reporting a decision the flatmate has not been asked about. A better message adds the exception, and a worse one explains why the split is equal rather than by size, which is the question a message of that length always provokes.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: The opening line of a cover letter for a post that asks for experience
questions.learningObjective: write an opening line inside a word limit and name what it does not do
questions.stem: Stage one: in no more than twenty-five words of Spanish, write the opening line of a cover letter for a post advertised as requiring two years of experience. Stage two: say what your opening line does not do, and why that matters in a letter read by somebody in a hurry.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: Con dos años de experiencia en atención al cliente, me dirijo a ustedes para solicitar el puesto de atención al cliente. Stage two: the opening line does not say what the two years were like, does not name a result, and does not say where the advertisement was seen, so the reader has three questions before the second line begins. That is the point of the format. A cover letter is a document with a reader who is holding several at once, and the first line exists to be the one that is read, so it should carry the number the advertisement asked for and the name of the post and nothing else. Me dirijo a ustedes is the formula for coming to write, and it keeps the register of the whole letter in a single choice of pronoun; a candidate who begins with a first name has changed the register of the document before a sentence has been completed. A better line would add a single phrase naming a measurable thing, and a worse one would apologise for a gap or explain a career change, which are the two openings that make a reader stop.

questions.hint: Ask what the advertisement asked for, and whether your first line says it.

questions.explanation: The first line of a cover letter is the only line that is certain to be read, and the answer should say so and then say what a first line can carry in twenty-five words. The useful content is the figure the advertisement asked for, the name of the post, and one register choice, and everything else belongs further down the page. A good answer will also name the two openings that make a reader stop, an apology for a gap and an explanation of a career change, and say that both are signals to a hurried reader that the candidate is managing their own feelings rather than answering the advertisement. The register point is the transferable one, since the formula used in the first line fixes the register of the whole document before a second sentence has been read.
